title: The two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28)
hook: the true mother gives up her claim to save the child

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon's request in a dream. Your line was a listening heart. Did you let someone finish before you decided? Today that heart gets its first hard case. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

Two women stand before the king, and there is one baby. They live in the same house. Nobody else was there. Each had a son, a few days apart. In the night one baby died, and now each woman says the living child is hers. There are no witnesses, no records, no way to check. One says, she switched them while I slept. The other says, no, the dead one is yours, the living one is mine. Back and forth, in front of the throne. And the new king, the one who asked for a listening heart, says something that silences the room: bring me a sword.
screen: `TWO WOMEN, ONE LIVING CHILD.` → `NO WITNESSES.` → `BRING ME A SWORD.`

segments.voice: The story is in First Kings, chapter three. The text calls the two women harlots and never gives their names. They come with no one to speak for them, and the king hears them anyway, in person. First, Solomon says both claims back, exactly: this one says the living son is hers and the dead one yours; that one says the opposite. He has listened. Then the sword is brought, and the order: divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other. Here's the turn. One woman cries out: give her the living child, and don't kill him. The text says she spoke because her compassion was stirred for her son. The Hebrew word is rachamim, compassion. The other woman says, in the 1917 Jewish translation, "It shall be neither mine nor thine; divide it." And the king answers: give the first woman the living child. She is his mother. Notice what he did. He didn't find new evidence. He made a moment where love would have to show itself, and it did, as giving way. The real mother was willing to lose the case to save the child. Then the text adds a line about everyone else: all Israel heard of the judgment, and saw that the wisdom of God was in the king, to do justice. There's a hard lesson inside the clever one. Sometimes the person who is right is the one willing to stop fighting. She didn't win by arguing better. She won by being ready to lose. And Solomon's listening heart heard the difference between someone who wanted the child and someone who only wanted to win.
screen: `TWO WOMEN WITH NO NAMES.` · `DIVIDE THE LIVING CHILD IN TWO.` · `GIVE HER THE CHILD. DON'T KILL HIM.` · `READY TO LOSE THE CASE.` · then, large: `IT SHALL BE NEITHER MINE NOR THINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give up winning to save something. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now: a family argument, a fight over credit at work, a back-and-forth that keeps going. Ask what's actually at stake underneath. A relationship? A child's peace? A friendship? Then ask: is there a way to let the argument go and keep the thing that matters? You don't have to decide yet. Just hold the two side by side, the win and the child. If you pray, you can ask for the heart to know the difference. The bell holds the time.
The two mothers. Two women, one living child, and a king who found the mother by watching who would give way. Today's word.
Your line: the real mother gives way. Today, in one small argument, let the point go if it saves something that matters more. Day seven hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews read the judgment of Solomon in the book of Kings, and the passage is assigned as the haftarah, the reading from the Prophets, for the Torah portion Miketz.

fork.reveal: she cried out to give the child to the other woman and not to kill him, and that is how Solomon knew she was his mother.

original.note: Hebrew: compassion. the real mother's rachamim was stirred for her son.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever trick with a sword.
what it means: Solomon made a moment where love had to show itself, and the real mother gave way.
what a scholar hears: the text says her rachamim, her compassion, was stirred, and gives the women no names, only a hearing.

notes: 'Her compassion was stirred' paraphrases 3:26 (nikhmeru rachameha); confirm the word rachamim there.
